https://www.dw.com/en/testosterone-and-f.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IBlH More men than ever are taking testosterone-boosting medication Image: BREUEL-BILD/IMAGO Advertisement Making sperm is, in large part, what testosterone is for. Which is why it is ironic when a man who doesn't need it starts taking it anyway: His brain registers an unusually high level of the hormone in his blood, concludes his body has made too much, and sends the order to stop. The testes go silent and sperm production declines. Testosterone is having a moment. It is all over social media, gym culture and wellness forums, sold by online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services. The information surrounding it ranges from oversimplified to outright dangerous. Men are taking more of it than ever, in pursuit of feeling more like men . In doing so, they may be telling their bodies to stop producing it themselves. Here is what the science says — what testosterone does, who genuinely needs treatment, and what it can cost the men who take it without needing it. How does taking testosterone stop sperm production? Your body regulates testosterone the way a thermostat regulates heat. When the brain detects abnormally high levels of the hormone in the bloodstream, it sends a signal to the testes to stop producing it naturally. The testes effectively go offline, and because sperm production depends on what happens inside them, that shuts down too. Some men who self-medicate with testosterone push their levels to more than four times the clinical lower threshold. The consequences include blood clotting disorders, cardiovascular stress, mood instability and, in some cases, irreversible fertility damage. What's sold as a shortcut to strength and libido can, unsupervised, cost a man his fertility. What are normal testosterone levels by age? Testosterone peaks during puberty, typically between 13 and 15. After that, it declines slowly for the rest of a man's life. A lower level at 40 than at 15 isn't a disorder — its aging. What counts as low testosterone? The threshold that doctors use is 300 nanograms per deciliter of blood. But this threshold comes with a condition: It must be confirmed by at least two blood tests taken at different times of the day, because levels fluctuate. Below that number, a doctor may begin to consider treatment. Above 300, there is no clinical basis for intervention. How can you increase testosterone naturally? Before any medical treatment is considered, four key lifestyle factors should be examined: sleep, alcohol consumption, smoking and drug use, and chronic stress. Each of these has a measurable impact on testosterone levels. Addressing them may be all that's needed and carries none of the risks of hormonal therapy. What is testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) and who actually needs it? Testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, treats a diagnosed hormonal deficiency. It's a legitimate medical procedure — involving injections, pills, creams — that works for men who need it. But plenty of men taking it don't have that deficiency. Men with normal testosterone levels are increasingly seeking TRT out anyway, not as a treatment but as a performance enhancer. They're getting it from unregulated online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services that write prescriptions without adequate medical assessment. Can testosterone therapy cause permanent infertility? In some cases, yes. Men who stop taking testosterone are likely to recover their own production within months. But not all of them. Depending on the dose and how long a man has been using, research puts the share who never recover at somewhere between one in ten and one in five. Low testosterone: What it does to men's health To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Does testosterone therapy actually work – or is it a placebo? Many men who self-administer testosterone report feeling stronger, sharper and more energetic. Some of that may reflect genuine physiological change. A significant portion is likely the placebo effect — a well-documented human tendency to feel better when we believe we are being treated. That does not make the feeling less real. It does mean that unsupervised hormonal intervention is a high-risk gamble for a benefit that may exist entirely in one's mind. The bottom line Doctors' advice is unambiguous: Get tested, know the number, and treat everything else — the websites, the influencers, the gym contacts — as anecdote, not medicine. A lot of men aren't waiting. Chasing peak masculinity online, they're reaching for the one substance that could tell their own bodies to stop making it. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz0z.text: Image source, Getty Images By Jonathan Beale Defence correspondent Published 6 hours ago Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe. Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance. But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new". They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West. The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia. Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader â saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory". Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing. However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts. They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation. Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries. Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role. It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this. Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil". Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine. The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns. Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home. They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power. Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties. The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit. That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/11/alge.text: Algeria has closed its airspace to Emirati-registered civilian and military aircraft after cutting diplomatic ties with the Gulf country on Thursday following years of tension.In a statement announcing the severing of diplomatic relations, Algiers accused the Gulf nation of "provocative and hostile acts", though the precise catalyst for the sudden rupture remained unclear.The Algerian defence ministry announced that an airspace ban targeting Emirati aircraft would take effect on Friday, with an exception for commercial flights to and from Algiers airport, which will be permitted to operate until the end of 2026.On Thursday, Algiers gave the UAE ambassador 48 hours "to comply with the decision" and leave the country.The Algerian foreign ministry stated the move came "after exhausting all avenues to preserve bilateral relations" with the UAE, noting it had issued repeated warnings to Abu Dhabi."Algeria spared no effort to draw the Emirati side's attention to, and to warn it against, the dire consequences that could result from its regrettable and unjustified conduct," the ministry said, adding that the UAE "persisted in its actions, reaching a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable".Emirati authorities expressed regret over the move, with the foreign ministry stating that it hoped the decision would prove temporary to maintain "fraternal ties" with Algeria."Wherever they set foot, blood flows"Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has frequently referred to the UAE as a "micro-state" seeking to destabilise regional nations, explicitly pointing to conflicts in Libya, Mali, and Sudan.In a televised interview in July, Tebboune launched a scathing critique of Abu Dhabi, asserting that "wherever they set foot, blood flows"."We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country," Tebboune added, noting at the time that a diplomatic break "would have happened long ago" had Algiers not sought to avoid "deepening divisions" within the Arab world.Tensions between the two countries have been fuelled by several developments in recent years, specifically as Algeria viewed the UAE's interference in North African and Sahelian affairs as contrary to its foreign policy principles and an indirect threat to Algerian security.Further divisions between Algiers and Abu Dhabi also stemmed from diverging diplomatic policies, including the UAE's normalisation of ties with Israel in 2020.
